cases.title: The deployment expert leaves in eleven weeks
cases.scenario:
Priya is the only person at Lumen, a 40-person payments company, who runs the weekly production deploy of the ledger service. She has given eleven weeks' notice. Eighteen months ago she wrote a 30-page runbook; the wiki shows it has been opened four times, twice by her. Two engineers, Dev and Marta, have each shadowed two deploys, sitting beside her while she typed.

The runbook contains steps nobody can explain. Step 14 is a 90-second wait before the cache flush; step 22 restarts a sidecar "twice, not once". Priya says the wait "was for something with the read replicas in 2023" and is not sure it still matters.

Tom, the engineering manager, has a plan and a budget line: Priya records a two-hour video walkthrough, expands the runbook to cover every step, and Dev and Marta watch the video before her last day. "Documentation is the deliverable," he says. "We can't afford to slow deploys while she's still here; we ship every Thursday."

Marta is uneasy. She can perform the steps but cannot say why any of them exist, and she has never done one without Priya in the room. Ten deploys remain before Priya leaves.
cases.question: How do you spend the ten remaining Thursdays, and what do you tell Tom about the video? Which two authors are arguing in your head?
considerations: Is the deploy a norm (its value depends on others doing it) or a skill with hidden causal structure? Which of Henrich's and Laland's mechanisms transfers each?
What did the stone-tool experiment find about imitation alone versus teaching with language, and how much weight does one modest study bear?
What does over-imitation predict Dev and Marta will do with step 14 once Priya is gone?
What should happen to the 90-second wait: keep, delete, or something else? Which book warns about removing "pointless" practices?
How would you count, separately, who can explain the deploy and who can do it?
cases.model_answer:
Decision: Dev and Marta run the next ten deploys themselves with Priya narrating reasons, and the video is cancelled. No strategic game here: a transmission problem, so first sort what is being transmitted. The deploy is a skill with hidden causal structure, not a norm, so t01's second branch applies: IF the target is a skill with non-obvious causal structure THEN budget for explicit teaching of reasons and put expiry dates on the playbooks. Laland's stone-tool result is the evidence: imitation added little over reverse engineering; teaching and language produced the largest gains (Morgan et al. 2015, verified, one study of 184 adults) [E for the mechanism; H for this domain].

Concretely: from Thursday, Dev and Marta drive the keyboard on alternate weeks while Priya sits behind them and speaks only in reasons ("we wait here because the replicas lag") [H, tested by whether they deploy alone by week eight]. Every opaque step gets a one-line "why" and a "review-by" date; the runbook becomes a checklist they edit after each run, so stale exemplars are discounted the way the tournament winner discounted old information [E as a simulation result; H as practice]. Step 14 is not deleted: Henrich's warning is to audit before removing a practice whose payoff may be delayed, so the wait gets an owner and a date to test against the replica-lag metric [H].

To Tom: the video is imitation with the model absent. Over-imitation predicts Dev and Marta will reproduce every step, including the wait, and lose the point the day a condition changes; that is t01's mirror error. Ten narrated deploys cost about what the video costs and produce two holders of the skill [E for isolation losing skills at lab scale; H at team scale]. Balancing measure: do not over-document; a young practice makes documentation overhead (`02`), so document reasons, not keystrokes [V, that a system beats a hero].

Switch signal: if by week six they reproduce the surface while incidents rise, teach more; if they can explain every step but will not deploy without Priya, the problem has become a norm of deference, and the lever is a visible model, not explanation. Register entry [H]: "two unaided deploys with no rollback by week eight; incident count in the quarter after Priya leaves no higher than the quarter before."
cases.novice_error: Accept Tom's plan, because a recorded walkthrough feels like the responsible artifact and costs Priya nothing on Thursdays. It transmits the surface of the practice perfectly and the reasons not at all, so the team keeps the ritual and loses the point. The mirror error is to strip out every unexplained step in the name of simplification before anyone has checked what the wait was for.

cases.title: "Quality first", then the March ship
cases.scenario:
In January, Lena, VP of Engineering at a 60-engineer analytics company, announced "quality first" at the all-hands: three principles on a slide, a poster in every office, a Slack channel. In March the CEO, Marcus, pushed the new Insights dashboard out for a customer conference on 14 March with 23 open bugs, two of them P1, over the objections of the team lead. The launch went fine commercially.

Since then the retro notes read the same every sprint: "tests skipped to hit the date." Two senior engineers, Ana and Yusuf, who other engineers visibly copy, have started approving PRs with failing checks because "that's apparently what we do now."

Lena's proposal, due to the leadership meeting on Monday, is a mandatory "quality week": a half-day training for every engineer on the three principles, a quiz, and a signed pledge. Marcus is fine with it as long as the April Exports feature ships on 22 April for a contract milestone. Ana, asked privately, says: "Nobody believes the poster any more. Another slide will make it worse."
cases.question: Do you back the quality week? If not, what do you put in its place before 22 April, and what do you tell Marcus?
considerations: In Henrich's terms, what did the 14 March ship transmit, and through which channel: the poster's or the CEO's?
Is "quality first" a norm or a skill, and what does t01 say adoption looks like for each?
What are Ana and Yusuf in the group's learning network, and what are they modelling now?
What would count as a credibility-enhancing display by Lena and Marcus, and what would it cost?
What must you not broadcast about how often builds ship broken (t10)?
cases.model_answer:
Decision: cancel the quality week and replace it with one visible, costly reversal by the two people the engineers watch most, before 22 April. Draw the situation first: "quality first" is a norm, not a skill; its value depends on everyone holding it and its payoff is diffuse. So t01's first branch applies: IF the target is a norm THEN put a prestigious, self-similar model visibly doing it and succeeding, make leaders' costly displays point the same way, and do not count a memo or training as adoption. The March ship was a credibility-enhancing display pointing the opposite way; one visible costly exception transmits the opposite norm (`01`) [E for the bias; H for the size of the effect here].

Three moves. First, Marcus and Lena publicly hold the Exports release on the first P1 found, and say so in the format they used in January: a display that costs a milestone carries the norm; a display that costs nothing is a poster [E for the mechanism; V that a real cost is the price of credibility]. Second, Ana and Yusuf, not the VP, are the visible refusers: two blocked merges by prestigious engineers, reasons written in the PR, do more than the training [E for prestige-biased copying; H for the intervention]. Third, fill the norm slot with a self-enforcing convention (`08`): merging on red is impossible by default, so the norm needs no daily heroism [E that conventions are cheaper to hold than social norms].

Balancing measure, from t10: never publish how many builds shipped broken; a count of misbehaviour is itself transmitted. Publish the sprints where every check passed, paired with visible approval [E for the pairing rule]. The pledge is dropped: a pledge for a norm nobody's models hold is a filing-cabinet norm.

To Marcus: 22 April is the test. If a P1 appears and the release ships anyway, the company has told 60 engineers, for the second time, what the norm is. Switch signal: if engineers can recite the principles and merge-on-red continues, the model channel is failing and needs more visible modelling; if skipped tests persist among those who never saw the reversal, the group is more than one reference network and the display must be repeated locally. Register entry [H]: "after one publicly held release, P1-with-known-bugs ships fall to zero for two quarters."
cases.novice_error: Run the quality week, because training is what you do when people "don't get it," and a quiz produces evidence of completion. Adoption is not a knowledge gap here; everyone knows the rule and watched it lose to a date. The mirror is to shame the March decision in public, which advertises how often quality loses and teaches the same lesson faster.

cases.title: The best-practices wiki nobody updates
cases.scenario:
Grainline is an open-source data-tooling project with about 400 contributors on record and 25 active in a typical month. It has a Best Practices wiki: 140 pages, median last edit 26 months ago. New contributors are told to read it in the welcome message. A survey Jonas, the lead maintainer, ran last month found that 8 of the 25 active contributors had read more than five pages, and that the three most-read pages were all out of date (the release process changed in 2024; the wiki describes the old one).

Jonas proposes a documentation sprint before the 3.0 release in six weeks: rewrite all 140 pages, then a rule that every pull request must cite the wiki page it follows, enforced by a bot. "If they don't read it, we make reading it the path of least resistance."

Wei, a long-tenured contributor whose PRs are the ones newcomers copy, says the opposite: delete the wiki, keep the three pages that matter, and stop pretending. A third maintainer points out that Wei's own PRs are the real style guide and always have been.
cases.question: Rewrite, delete, or something else, and what happens to Jonas's citation rule? What do you decide before the 3.0 release?
considerations: Of the 140 pages, which are norms (review etiquette, style) and which are hidden-structure skills (release, migrations)? Does t01 give them the same channel?
What did the tournament winner do with old information, and what is the wiki doing with it?
Why are Wei's PRs the real style guide, and what does that say about the channel norms travel through?
What is the citation rule, in game terms: assurance, enforcement, or a costly signal? On which problem?
What does Laland say happens to a population of pure copiers, and what does that imply for an exemplar-based guide?
cases.model_answer:
Decision: neither rewrite nor delete. Triage the 140 pages into two kinds, give each its own channel, and drop the citation rule. Draw the situation first: there is no defector to sanction; a transmission channel has silted up. The wiki does the opposite of the tournament's winning strategy: it keeps old information at full weight instead of discounting it (Rendell et al. 2010, verified, 104 entries, a simulation) [E as a model result; H for this project]. So the first move is Laland's "expire old exemplars": every page gets a date and an owner, and any page without an owner by the 3.0 release is archived with its date visible [H].

Then the split, t01's rule: IF the target is a norm THEN put a prestigious model visibly doing it; IF it is a skill with hidden causal structure THEN teach the reasons. Pages that describe norms (how we review, how we name things) are replaced by visible models: the page becomes a link to three recent exemplar PRs, two of them Wei's. Norm adherence spreads through models and prestige, and explanation is a weak channel for it; the third maintainer has already told you Wei's PRs are the style guide [E for the mechanism; H for the intervention]. Pages that describe skills with hidden causal structure (release, migrations, security disclosure) are kept, rewritten by their owners, and paired with a narrated walkthrough on a recorded release call, where teaching and language beat imitation (Morgan et al. 2015, verified, one study) [E for the mechanism; H for transfer]. Everything else is archived.

Jonas's citation rule is enforcement aimed at a transmission problem: a bot demanding a citation manufactures a ritual (cite the page, ignore it). Balancing measure: a project of pure copiers stagnates, so one page is "experiments we are running," and maintainers reserve review time for contributions that break the exemplar on purpose (`02`) [E in the tournament; V that innovation is worth some review cost, Jonas dissenting].

Switch signal: if after 3.0 newcomers' PRs match the exemplars but the release still breaks in anyone's hands but Jonas's, teach more; if the release process is understood but only its authors follow the review norms, the model channel needs a more visible model. Register entry [H]: "by 3.1, at least three maintainers have run a release unaided, and the share of first PRs needing style rework falls."
cases.novice_error: Fund the rewrite, because 140 fresh pages look like diligence and a bot rule looks like rigour. Both treat adoption as reading, and the survey already showed reading is not happening. Deleting everything feels honest but throws away the few pages whose reasons cannot be copied from a PR.

cases.title: Twelve people, two "coasters", and a leaderboard
cases.scenario:
The platform team at Corvid grew from 5 to 12 engineers in nine months. Sam, the manager, has a chart: merged changes per engineer per sprint are down by about a quarter since the team was 5, while total output is flat. He has names: Rick and Jo, both hired in the growth wave, "coast." Performance reviews are in five weeks.

Sam's fix is ready to deploy: an individual story-point leaderboard shown at every standup, and a quarterly bonus tied to points. "Visibility fixes this. People rise to what's measured."

Ola, the tech lead, objects that this has always been a communal team: people pick up reviews, mentor the new hires and fix each other's bugs without being asked, and none of that shows in story points. She also notes that the team still runs one shared board with one shared backlog; nobody owns any component, and a change to the ingestion service last month had four authors and no reviewer who felt responsible. Rick, asked about his numbers, says he spent most of the last two sprints unblocking the data team.
cases.question: Do you ship the leaderboard? If not, what do you do about output per head, and about Rick and Jo, before the review cycle?
considerations: What does a 12-person team with one backlog and no ownership look like in game terms? Which social-psychology effect does that structure produce, and is it dispositional?
What does the course say to check before concluding "we have free-riders"?
What does a partial metric (points) do to the unmeasured effort (reviews, mentoring, unblocking)? Which book states this as theory?
What is the evidence on introducing scorekeeping into a communal relationship, and on bonuses as a lever for positive reciprocity?
If the structure is fixed and two people still contribute little, which tension takes over?
cases.model_answer:
Decision: no leaderboard and no individual bonus; restructure into three pods of four with named ownership, make effort visible as a by-product of the work, and only then look at Rick and Jo. Draw the game first: twelve people, one backlog, one shared output and no identifiable contribution is a public-goods game with unidentifiable effort, and that structure produces loafing whoever is in it (`03`, on the robust list) [E]. The course's rule is to diagnose situationally before dispositionally, because the attribution error is among the best-replicated findings in the book [E].

t12's rule: IF the behaviour is one you want members to own (review, mentoring, unblocking) THEN use small public commitments, modest recognition and norms; never introduce individual scorekeeping into a communal team without expecting damage, and if a metric is needed make it collective [E for the mechanism; H for this team]. Dixit adds the theory: a partial metric displaces the unmeasured effort that shares its budget, and Rick's last two sprints are that effort [E as theory; H for magnitude]. The bonus is the weakest lever: positive reciprocity to extra pay boosted effort for the first few hours only and cost more than it returned (Gneezy and List 2006, verified) [E].

Concretely: three pods of four (the `03` figure of 2-5 is a rule of thumb, not a measured optimum) [H], each owning named services; and the Balancing measure, since a PD must never run on norms alone: monitoring as a by-product (CODEOWNERS, reviewer of record) with any metric collective, per pod [E for the principle; H for transfer]. Write the BPC table for Rick and Jo before the review (`11`): Rick's answer is already a constraint, not a preference [E as bookkeeping]. Whether this team is a community or a set of exchange partners is the value under the decision [V, with Sam dissenting].

Switch signal: if after a quarter of identifiable pods the same two are stable, identifiable non-contributors, t05's self-interested tail is in play and t02's cheap graduated sanctions apply; if the measured behaviour rises and reviews fall, the metric is displacing and goes. To Sam: the leaderboard buys points and sells the mentoring you did not measure. Register entry [H]: "with pods and ownership, per-head throughput recovers within two quarters without a leaderboard; reviews per engineer do not fall."
cases.novice_error: Ship the leaderboard, because it is the product default (instrument it, rank it) and it visibly "does something" before the review cycle. It converts a communal team into an exchange one and rewards the measurable half of the work. The mirror is to refuse all measurement out of trust, so the two who genuinely coast stay invisible and the conditional cooperators quietly stop.

cases.title: The banner that made direct pushes worse
cases.scenario:
Farah runs the internal developer platform for 180 engineers. The rule is that nothing goes to `main` without a reviewed pull request. In May she counted 37 direct pushes and put a red banner on the CI dashboard everyone opens each morning: "Last month: 37 direct pushes to main. Please stop." In June there were 52.

Her next proposal, for the July platform meeting, is a bigger banner with the names of the engineers who pushed directly, refreshed daily. "If shame doesn't work, more shame will." A staff engineer, Kwame, says the banner is the problem, not the fix, but cannot say why in a way that convinces her. The raw numbers, which Farah has not put on the banner: about 2,400 changes reached `main` in June, so around 98% went through review. Of the 52 direct pushes, 31 came from four people on one team that runs hotfixes for a legacy service without a working PR pipeline.
cases.question: What goes on the dashboard in July, and what do you do about the four engineers and the legacy team?
considerations: Which channel did the May banner use, descriptive or injunctive, and what did it tell the 176 engineers who never push directly?
What did the Petrified Forest sign and the energy-feedback studies show about advertising the frequency of misbehaviour?
Is reviewed-merging the majority's behaviour here? What does t10 say to publish when it is?
What does a names banner do without a legitimate process (t02)?
Are the 31 pushes from one team a norm problem at all?
cases.model_answer:
Decision: take the banner down, publish the 98% with a visible approval signal, fix the legacy team's pipeline, and refuse the names board. Draw the situation: a near-universal convention with a small pocket of deviance, and the May banner told 176 compliant engineers that direct pushes are common. That is the boomerang: descriptive feedback alone pulls people above the norm down toward it, as the energy-feedback experiments found, and the theft sign in the Petrified Forest raised theft (`03`) [E for the boomerang]; "most people don't do this" is itself transmitted (`01`) [E].

t10's first branch applies: IF the target behaviour is already the majority's THEN publish the count and pair it with a visible approval signal. So the July dashboard reads "98% of changes to main last month went through review," with a line from the two most-copied staff engineers saying that is how it should be: descriptive and injunctive channels pointing the same way (ledger #24) [E for the pairing rule; H for its size here].

The four engineers are a structural problem, not a norm problem: 31 of 52 pushes come from a team whose PR pipeline does not work for hotfixes, so their behaviour is a constraint, not a belief or a preference (`11`'s BPC bookkeeping) [E as a discipline]. Fix the pipeline first. Balancing measure, so the descriptive channel never runs alone, t02: a cheap, fast, proportionate channel (a bot comment on any direct push that opens a retroactive PR and pings the author), with a written escalation ladder, and branch protection as the structural backstop [E for graduated sanctions in durable institutions; H for this platform].

The names board is refused on two grounds: it is descriptive again, with a shaming twist, and public peer punishment without a legitimate process is where antisocial punishment starts [E for the sensitivity; V for the constraint, with Farah dissenting]. To Farah: the banner did not fail because it was small; it worked, and it taught the wrong count.

Switch signal: run the four-question elicitation before and after July. If above-norm engineers regress after the 98% is published, or people can state the count and still do not believe anyone expects a PR, the normative channel needs backing from t02's ladder. Register entry [H]: "direct pushes fall below 15 a month within two months of pipeline fix plus paired messaging, without a names board."
cases.novice_error: Make the banner bigger and add names, because the first one "didn't work" and escalation feels like resolve. The first one worked exactly as the evidence predicts; it broadcast a minority behaviour as common. The mirror error is to delete the banner and say nothing, leaving the legacy team's pipeline broken and the count to drift.

cases.title: The hiring committee that wants bias training
cases.scenario:
Vantage, a 300-person company, has a seven-member engineering hiring committee. All seven studied at the same two universities and came up through backend work. Of the last 20 hires, 18 fit the same profile. Interview debriefs run as open discussion, chaired by Ravi, the most senior member, who usually opens with his read of the candidate; the vote is a show of hands.

Dana, Head of People, has a proposal for the end of the quarter: a half-day implicit-bias training built around the Implicit Association Test for all 40 interviewers, plus a values session on "our inclusive culture." Ravi supports it: "It's cheap and it shows we care." A founder on the committee says the opposite: "Hire for fit; culture is why we ship."

Two hiring managers outside the committee have complained that strong candidates from other pipelines (a bootcamp partnership, two internal transfers from data) were rejected after debriefs in which the first speaker was negative and nobody dissented. The next committee cycle begins in three weeks with 14 candidates.
cases.question: Do you fund Dana's training? What do you change about the committee before the 14 debriefs, and what do you tag as a value?
considerations: What does the ledger say about IAT-based training, and which intergroup intervention does have moderate evidence?
Is the 18-of-20 pattern evidence of bias or of selection and homophily? What does the course assume by default?
What does a homogeneous group do when it deliberates, and what structural fixes does `03` give?
Which of t08's poles is Dana's proposal, and which pole does the rule say to build first?
What does "hire for fit" do to a learning network over time (`01`)?
cases.model_answer:
Decision: decline the IAT-based training, restructure the debrief before the 14 candidates, add two committee members from outside the cluster, and write the goal down as a value. Draw the situation: no opponent, but a deliberating group whose composition and procedure push the same way. Assume selection over influence for the 18-of-20 similarity (ledger #35) [E as a default]; homogeneous groups polarize when they deliberate (`03`) [E]; Ravi speaking first makes each debrief a sequential public signal, the cascade setup of `10` ch 16 [E for the mechanism].

t08's rule: IF you are choosing between an identity intervention and a within-group mechanism THEN build the within-group mechanism first and treat identity work as an accelerant tagged [H]. Dana's proposal is identity work of the weakest kind: IAT-based training is on the ledger's do-not-build list (#20), while structured contact around shared goals has a reliable moderate effect across 500+ studies (Pettigrew and Tropp 2006, background; rigorous field experiments fewer and smaller) [E for contact; not [E] for the training]. The mechanism is procedural: written independent scores before discussion, revealed together; Ravi speaks last; one assigned credible dissenter; proposal separated from evaluation (`03`, `10`) [E for each mechanism; H for the package]. Then t09: two members from the data organization and the bootcamp partnership as bridges into the rejected pipelines [H for the mix], and a shared calibration task between interviewers and those pipelines' hiring managers, the contact form with evidence [E moderate].

To Ravi: "it shows we care" is a display aimed at the wrong channel. To the founder: a network that hires only self-similar copies narrows what the collective brain retains (`01`) [E at lab scale; H here]. Whether profile diversity is a goal at all is a value; write it as one, with the founder named as dissenter [V]. Balancing measure: procedure fixes deliberation, not sourcing; if the pipelines carry one profile, no debrief rule changes the hires.

Switch signal: if two cycles of private-first scoring give the same profile share, the problem is upstream in sourcing; if identification with "our inclusive culture" rises while hires do not change, identity work has run without a mechanism. Register entry [H]: "with private scores first and two outside members, non-standard-profile hires among the next 20 exceed 2 of 20."
cases.novice_error: Fund the training, because it is cheap, visible, and hard to argue against in a leadership meeting. It builds on a method the ledger lists as not to be built on and leaves the debrief structure, which is doing the damage, untouched. The mirror is the founder's: declare fit a virtue and never notice that the committee's unanimity is fast and wrong.

cases.title: Forty people saw the checksum post
cases.scenario:
Sable is an open-source cryptography library with a community Slack of about 2,000 members and nine maintainers. At 09:12 on a Tuesday a new user posted in `#general`: "The 4.2.1 tarball checksum doesn't match the one on the site. Is this a compromise or am I doing something wrong?" Slack's view count reached 40 by 10:00. Three people added a thinking-face emoji. Nobody replied. Ines, a maintainer, saw the post at 15:30, verified within twenty minutes that a mirror was serving a stale file, and posted a fix at 16:10. Seven hours of silence on a possible supply-chain compromise.

Ines's diagnosis, in the maintainers' channel that evening: "People just don't care. We need a security champion role and a code-of-conduct clause: if you see a security concern you are required to report it." The 4.3 release is in three weeks. Another maintainer, Bruno, points out that at least six of the 40 viewers were experienced contributors who would have known how to check a checksum in two minutes.
cases.question: What do you build before the 4.3 release, and is Ines's "people don't care" a preference or a belief?
considerations: What does the bystander literature say is robust, and in which settings? Which three ingredients were present at 09:12?
Write the BPC table for one of the six experienced viewers: what did they believe about the other 39?
Does a code-of-conduct clause change a constraint, a preference or a belief? Which column did the failure live in?
What are `03`'s four bystander fixes, and which of them are structural?
How would you know whether the fix worked before the next real alarm?
cases.model_answer:
Decision: build the structure that removes ambiguity and diffusion of responsibility before 4.3, and drop the code-of-conduct clause. Draw the situation: forty people, one ambiguous signal ("or am I doing something wrong?"), no named owner, and everyone able to see that nobody else had replied. That is the bystander structure, [E] precisely for ambiguous, low-risk-looking situations (ledger #23); in obvious emergencies someone almost always acts. The thinking-face emoji are pluralistic ignorance in miniature.

t11's rule sorts the fix. Nothing about the six experienced viewers' preferences changed between 09:12 and 16:10; what differed was what each believed the others had done. IF behaviour moves with the order of information or the first rounds THEN treat it as a belief: change the information and the first response, not the payoffs. The BPC table (`11`) for Bruno's six reads: beliefs, "someone closer will handle this"; preferences, they care; constraints, none. Ines's clause changes the constraint column for a failure in the belief column, the usual error the rule names [E for BPC as bookkeeping; H for its predictive value here]. The `03` fixes are structural [E for each mechanism; H for the package]: make the problem unambiguous (a `#security-reports` channel with a template); assign named ownership (a rotating maintainer-of-the-week in the channel topic); give a script ("reply 'checking', run the verify command"); make the first move cheap (one emoji pages the maintainer of the week). The champion role is fine if it is the rota, not a hero.

To Ines: "people don't care" is the dispositional reading the course tests last; the same six would have acted in a channel with a name on it. Balancing measure: the belief pole has a floor. If reports still do not come once ownership is fixed, the residual is a cost, fear of being wrong in front of 2,000 people, and that is a payoff to change: thank false alarms publicly [H]. That false alarms are welcome is a value; say so [V, Ines dissenting].

Switch signal: toward beliefs, confirmed, if a drill produces a reply within minutes from someone silent on Tuesday; toward preferences if, with ownership and script in place, experienced viewers still wait. Register entry [H]: "time to first substantive reply on a planted security report under 15 minutes, twice, before 4.3 ships."
cases.novice_error: Write the clause and appoint a champion, because a rule and a title look like accountability and take an evening. The clause obligates 2,000 people who already wanted to help and were each waiting for someone else; the champion becomes the one person everyone now waits for. The mirror is to conclude that Slack is simply the wrong channel and move security to email, which makes the next report invisible instead of ambiguous.

cases.title: The maintenance day that needs eight
cases.scenario:
The Halden Street tool library is a member-run commons: 120 households pay a small annual fee and borrow tools. Once a month a maintenance day sharpens, repairs and inventories the stock. It needs eight volunteers to get through the list; with fewer, the day ends with half the work undone and everyone who came feeling their Saturday was wasted. Attendance over the last four months: 9, 7, 5, 4.

Bea, the coordinator, has drafted a rule for the members' meeting in three weeks: every household must attend two maintenance days a year, and no-shows have their borrowing suspended for a month. "Volunteering is dead. People respond to obligations."

Karl, who has attended every session, disagrees: "People want to come. They just don't know if anyone else is coming, so they don't bother. Send a reminder." The next maintenance day is twelve days after the meeting, and the inventory list already shows nine tools waiting on repairs that only get done on those Saturdays.
cases.question: What rule, if any, do you propose at the meeting, and what do you do about the next maintenance day?
considerations: Does a household gain by staying home when eight others show up? Does it gain by staying home when only four will? What game is that?
Where is the critical mass, and what happens to a shared practice launched or continued below it (`05`)?
What are the assurance devices `04` and `07` name, and which is cheapest to try in twelve days?
If attendance recovers after an assurance device and then decays again, what has the decay told you?
What does Ostrom say about matching obligations to benefits, if a rule is eventually needed?
cases.model_answer:
Decision: no obligation rule at this meeting; propose a threshold launch with public pledges for the next maintenance day, and hold Bea's rule in reserve with a stated trigger. Draw the game with t07's diagnostic: does a household gain by staying home when everyone else comes? Slightly. But the dominant fact runs the other way: with four present, coming is a wasted Saturday, so each household's willingness depends on believing others will come. That is a stag hunt with a critical mass at eight, not a prisoner's dilemma [E for the formal distinction; H for this group's classification]. Four months of decline is Schelling's half-launch, which decays and poisons the next attempt through self-defeating expectations [H].

The rule's first branch applies: IF nobody gains by defecting against full cooperation THEN build assurance and stop building enforcement: public pledges, threshold launches, a leader naming the target. For the day twelve days out: a public sign-up list reading "the day runs if eight households sign up by Wednesday; otherwise it is cancelled and nobody wastes a Saturday" [E for threshold devices in `04`; H here]; Bea names the target; Karl, who has attended every session, is the visible model. The cancellation clause makes the pledge credible by removing the wasted-Saturday cost of being the lone cooperator, the lever that moves the watershed most (t04) [E for the model].

Balancing measure, and the answer to Bea: run the talk first because it is cheap, and watch the following rounds. If attendance recovers to eight and holds, it was assurance. If it recovers and then sags month by month with the same households absent, decay is the prisoner's-dilemma signature and the second branch applies: a graduated obligation matched to benefits as Ostrom's cases do, with a small first sanction, never a month's suspension [E for graduated sanctions in durable commons; H for transfer]. Suspension as a first strike would land on households that were merely uncertain. Whether the library should ever compel attendance is a value [V, Bea dissenting]. To Karl: a reminder tells people the date, not that others are coming; the sign-up list tells them that.

Switch signal: cooperation at the meeting against cooperation three sessions later. Register entry [H]: "with a threshold sign-up, the next three maintenance days each reach eight; if any falls below six without cancellation, the obligation rule goes to the next meeting."
cases.novice_error: Pass Bea's rule, because falling numbers look like free-riding and an obligation with teeth feels like taking the problem seriously. It installs monitoring and penalties on people who were waiting to be assured, and the suspension will land on the uncertain rather than the unwilling. The mirror, Karl's, is to send another reminder and treat the fourth decline as bad luck.

cases.title: Ban or note?
cases.scenario:
Fernhill is a hobbyist electronics forum with about 5,000 members and six volunteer moderators. Its code of conduct has a "zero tolerance" clause: demeaning remarks lead to a permanent ban. On Monday a member with the handle Tarn, two years on the forum, about 800 posts, most of them helpful, told a newcomer their question was "the kind of thing people ask when they shouldn't own a soldering iron." The newcomer deleted their account. A complaint thread has 30 replies, several of them abusive toward Tarn.

Policy gives the moderators 48 hours to decide. Two moderators want the permanent ban: "The clause says what it says; if we don't apply it, the CoC is theatre." Lucia, the longest-serving moderator, wants a private note to Tarn and nothing public: "He's one of our best people; a ban loses him and gains nothing." The remaining three are undecided and, privately, exhausted: in the last year the team has applied the ban clause once and quietly ignored eleven reported violations because nobody wanted to be the one who pulled the trigger.
cases.question: Ban, note, or something else by Wednesday, and what do you do about the eleven ignored reports and the abusive thread?
considerations: What is the sanction in game terms: is a permanent ban a credible threat when the enforcers avoid applying it? What does `04` say about sanctions that cost the enforcer too much?
What do Ostrom's durable commons do for a first violation, and what does the 91-study review say about it?
Was Tarn's remark an unfair intention or an unlucky outcome, and what does `06` say that predicts about the newcomer's exit and the thread?
What is the 30-reply thread, in t02's terms, and what does the course say about peer punishment without a process?
What ladder would the six moderators actually apply?
cases.model_answer:
Decision: a graduated, public, quick sanction now, a published ladder by the end of the week, and the zero-tolerance clause rewritten. Draw the game first: a repeated game with reputation, in which a sanction deters only if credible, and a sanction that costs the enforcer more than ignoring the violation will not be applied and will not deter (`04`) [E]. One ban and eleven ignored reports in a year prove it: the permanent ban is a nuclear first strike six volunteers will not fire, so Fernhill has no sanctions in practice.

t02's rule: IF you are budgeting enforcement THEN assume members sanction only when the channel is cheap, fast and proportionate, and make the ladder known. Ostrom's durable cases use graduated sanctions, small and quick and public first, supported in the 91-study review (Cox et al. 2010, verified) [E for the field pattern; H for transfer to a digital forum, scope flagged]. So by Wednesday: a moderator reply in the thread naming the rule Tarn broke, a seven-day posting restriction, and an entry in a public sanctions log [E for the mechanism; H for this calibration]. The rewrite: a three-step ladder (public note and short restriction; longer restriction; ban) with a fast track for flagrant cases and a cheap channel where Tarn can contest the step [E for dispute forums in Ostrom's principles; H for transfer].

The newcomer's exit and the pile-on are one phenomenon: people punish intended unfairness far more than unlucky outcomes (`06`, Blount 1995) [E in the lab]. The thread is peer punishment without a process, where antisocial punishment starts; close it [E for the sensitivity; V that legitimacy constrains peer sanction, the two ban-minded moderators dissenting]. To Lucia: a private note keeps the sanction invisible, and punishment works largely through what observers learn (`02`) [E/H]. Balancing measure: the ladder must have a top and the fast track must be real, because the mirror error is removing sanctions and watching contributions decay as Camerer's curves predict.

Switch signal: count violations reported against violations sanctioned, and by whom. If the ratio stays near one in twelve, the first step is still too costly and needs a one-click template; if moderators pay visible personal costs and violations still climb, escalate. Register entry [H]: "at least three of every four reported violations receive a first-step sanction within 48 hours over the next quarter."
cases.novice_error: Apply the ban, because the clause is written and consistency sounds like fairness. The ban is applied so rarely that consistency is the one thing it lacks, and it would be applied here mainly because the thread demanded it. The mirror, Lucia's, keeps a valued member by making the sanction invisible, which teaches 5,000 observers that reports go nowhere.

cases.title: "We've played this game for years"
cases.scenario:
Amir founded a shared machine-learning compute cooperative three years ago with nine research labs. Members submit jobs to a common queue with a priority flag; the founding norm was that you flag a job urgent only when it is. In year one about 5% of jobs were flagged urgent. The co-op now has 70 member groups, and last quarter 30% of jobs were flagged urgent; queue-jumping complaints reach the ops lead, Hana, weekly, and two founding labs have started overstating their own priorities "because everyone does."

The compute grant that funds the cluster is up for renewal in two months, and the funder has asked how the co-op governs itself. Hana wants automated per-group quotas enforced by the scheduler, designed and deployed by ops. Amir is against any rule: "We've played this game for years. Repeat interaction guarantees cooperation. Rules would insult the labs that built this." Two of the newer member groups, asked privately, say they overstate because they have never met anyone from the labs whose jobs they are jumping.
cases.question: Is Amir right about repeat play? What do you propose to the funder, and what does the scheduler enforce?
considerations: At nine labs, who observed whom, and how fast was an overstated priority detected? At 70, what is the shadow of the future between any two groups?
What does the ledger say repetition guarantees, and what problems does it leave unsolved (#15)?
Which of t14's rules applies to a behaviour that depends on observation and sanctions?
What does nesting look like for a compute queue, and what is the higher layer for?
Is Hana's quota a designed rule or a self-governed one (t06), and what does that predict about compliance?
cases.model_answer:
Decision: Amir is right about year one and wrong about year three; nest the co-op into pods of about ten groups, make queue behaviour visible inside each pod, and hand the quota rule to the pods rather than the scheduler. Draw the game first: overstating priority when others are honest pays, so this is a prisoner's dilemma at the margin, an open-access commons [E]. At nine labs every group saw every other's jobs and each pair had years of dealings ahead, so repetition with fast detection made honesty one equilibrium (`04`) [E for the folk-theorem logic]. At 70 groups no pair meets often and who punishes whom is hard; every mechanism the founders relied on weakened as the group grew [E].

t14's rule: IF a behaviour depends on mutual observation or on sanctions THEN keep the unit small, bounded and stable, and scale by nesting: local units govern local problems, a higher layer handles conflict between units and shared infrastructure. Concretely: seven pods of about ten groups with a steward each; each pod gets a share of the cluster and a visible pod-level queue, so an urgent flag is seen by nine groups who share its consequence, monitoring as a by-product of use (`09`) [E for the principle in bounded field cases; H for transfer to a digital commons, scope flagged]. Each pod sets its urgent share within a cluster-wide cap, with a graduated automatic first sanction: an urgent job that finishes with idle time lowers the group's priority next week [E for graduated sanctions; H for this design]. Boundaries are written down: who is in, what they owe, who is excluded and why [V, because a boundary that makes monitoring work also excludes].

To Hana: an ops-designed quota imposed on 70 groups is followed while enforced (t06; Cardenas, background) [E for the pattern]. To Amir: repeat play is what the co-op had at nine; at 70 it must be rebuilt in units where people meet. Balancing measure: pods must not become guilds; the higher layer keeps admission open.

Switch signal: urgent-flag share per pod against pod size, and fraction of flagged violations sanctioned; if pods above a dozen drift back toward 30% while smaller ones hold, the unit is still too large. Register entry [H]: "urgent-flag share below 10% cluster-wide within two quarters of nesting, without scheduler-enforced quotas."
cases.novice_error: Take Amir at his word, because the founders' cooperation is real and rules feel like an insult to it. Their cooperation was produced by a structure that no longer exists at 70. The mirror is Hana's: a central quota written by ops, which converts a community into a rule it will spend its ingenuity gaming.

cases.title: The Friday demo that went from twelve to three
cases.scenario:
Nadia, head of product at a 15-team company, started a Friday cross-team demo in January. Twelve teams presented in the first month. Four months later, three teams present and about ten people attend. Presenting takes each team about two hours of preparation, and a team that presents to ten people gets little back; a team that attends when nobody presents has lost an hour. The three still presenting are the ones whose demos led to decisions being taken in the room.

Nadia's plan, for Monday's leadership meeting: attendance mandatory for every team lead, an attendance list emailed to the executive team each week, and a catered lunch. "It worked when everyone came. We just need everyone to come."

Ravi, one of the three still presenting, says the mandate will fill the room with people on laptops and that the demo died because teams stopped believing anyone would be there. He has no counter-proposal beyond "give it time."
cases.question: Do you support the mandate? What would you do instead to get the demo back above the point where it sustains itself?
considerations: Draw the payoffs: when is presenting worth two hours, and what is the cost of being one of the few who prepared? Which equilibrium is the group in now?
What does Schelling say happens to a practice that runs below its critical mass for months?
t04 lists cheap correlation levers in order. Which one attacks the cost of the lone cooperator, and which merely sweetens the joint payoff?
What are the three remaining teams, structurally, and how would you grow from them?
What does a mandate change about the lone-cooperator payoff?
cases.model_answer:
Decision: no mandate; cut the cost of presenting to near zero, let the three teams be the visible core, and grow the demo back from a smaller, stable unit. Draw the game first: each team's payoff from presenting depends on how many others attend and present; above a critical mass the room is worth two hours, below it presenting is a loss. That is a stag hunt with a threshold, settled in the risk-dominant equilibrium where staying away is safe; under random attendance, a large group and no channel for commitment, that is the predicted default (ledger #2) [E for the model and the coordination lab].

t04's rule: IF you can create correlation THEN do the cheap things first, in order: lower the cost of being the lone cooperator, have a leader publicly name the target, take public opt-in pledges, grow from a small core with a visible success record, keep neighbourhoods small and stable while the norm is young. So: demos become five-minute unrehearsed screen-shares, so presenting to ten people costs nothing [E for the model; H that preparation is the binding cost]. Nadia names the target, "five teams by end of month" (`06`, a leader naming the target selects the efficient equilibrium) [E]. A public sign-up for four Fridays is the pledge [E for cheap talk in stag hunts; H here]. A five-team pod demo for a month, then merge: gradual growth from a core (Weber 2006, verified, single lab) [E in the lab; H here].

To Nadia: the mandate raises attendance without changing the cost of presenting, producing a room of laptops and confirming the presenters' belief that nobody is there for them; the lunch sweetens the joint payoff, the weakest lever. Whether the demo is worth fifteen teams' Friday hour is a value [V, Nadia's mandate the dissent]. Balancing measure: structure can hold the good equilibrium while beliefs stay fragile (`07`), so take a public commitment from the five before opening to fifteen.

Switch signal: watch the lone-cooperator payoff directly; if presenting teams are visibly worse off than absent ones after the format change, shrink the pods again; if the adopting fraction rises past the point where switching pays, the levers are working. Register entry [H]: "at least five teams present unprompted on four consecutive Fridays within six weeks of the five-minute format."
cases.novice_error: Mandate attendance and cater lunch, because the demo "worked when everyone came" and a full room looks like the January state. The room was never the problem; the belief that the room would be there was, and a mandated audience does not restore it. The mirror is Ravi's patience, which waits for a decayed practice to recover from an equilibrium it will not leave on its own.

cases.title: ADRs stuck at two teams for a year
cases.scenario:
Twelve months ago the architecture group at a 90-engineer company adopted architecture decision records: a short document per significant decision, kept in the repository. Two of nine teams, Platform and Data, write one for every decision and read each other's. The other seven "tried it once." A count of the last quarter: Platform 14 ADRs, Data 11, the rest 3 in total. Engineers on the seven say the records are not worth writing because nobody on their side reads them, and not worth reading because nobody on their side writes them.

Noor, a staff engineer, proposes adding "ADR written" to the company-wide definition of done, checked at sprint review. The CTO prefers an "ADR champion" in every team, one person trained to evangelise. Platform's lead notes that the two adopting teams share a floor and review each other's code; the other seven are on other floors and mostly review within their own team.
cases.question: Which proposal do you back, or what do you do instead, to get ADRs past two teams this quarter?
considerations: Write the payoffs: what is the value of an ADR to a team when its neighbours write and read them, and when they do not? What is q here?
What is the Platform-Data pair, structurally, and why has the norm not spread from it?
Is ADR-writing a simple or a complex contagion? What does that say about one champion per team?
Which of the `10` levers lowers q, which seeds, and which builds bridges? Which applies to which team?
What does t06 predict about a rule added to the definition of done by the architecture group?
cases.model_answer:
Decision: neither the mandate nor the champions; lower the cost of writing an ADR, seed inside the most connected resisting team, and build several parallel ties between Platform-Data and that team. Draw the game first: an ADR pays a team only when enough of the teams it works with also write and read them. That is a coordination game on a network; a node switches when its fraction of adopting neighbours exceeds q = b/(a+b), a theorem in `10`, and seven teams sit below q in clusters dense enough to block a norm from outside, while the Platform-Data cluster protects it inside (ledger #3) [E for the theorem; H for the actual q].

t04's rule applies, IF you can create correlation THEN do the cheap things first, with t09's structural levers. Lower q: a one-page template in every repository, an ADR auto-linked from any PR touching a listed directory (`10`) [E in the model; H for size]. Seed inside: the team among the seven that ships most against Platform gets two Platform engineers pair-reviewing with it for a quarter, writing ADRs jointly; a cluster blocks only while none of its members has switched [E, theorem]. Widen the bridge: ADR-writing is a costly behaviour, a complex contagion needing several adopting neighbours; it does not cross one weak tie (ledger #34) [E for the direction]. The CTO's single champion per team is one weak tie: information crosses, behaviour does not.

To Noor: a definition-of-done rule imposed by the architecture group on seven teams gets compliance while checked and a two-line ADR at sprint review (t06) [E for the pattern; H here]; hold it in reserve. Balancing measure: do not scatter the Platform-Data pocket to evangelise, the t09 mistake; and publish the decisions where an ADR saved a reversal, so success is copied (ledger #36) [H]. Whether every decision needs a record is a value the seven teams should be asked, not told [V, Noor dissenting].

Switch signal (t13): if after q is lowered and the seed team adopts, the remaining six still do not, and their engineers can state the norm and believe nobody expects it of them, the residue is an expectations problem inside one floor, and the lever becomes publishing the gap. Register entry [H]: "a third team writes at least eight ADRs in the quarter after seeding; a fourth follows within two quarters without a mandate."
cases.novice_error: Add it to the definition of done, because a checkbox reaches all nine teams at once and can be reported upward. It reaches them as someone else's rule, and it will be met with the thinnest document that passes the check. The mirror is the champion model, which sends one person into each dense cluster and expects a costly habit to cross a single tie.

cases.title: The seniors all ended up on Core
cases.scenario:
Bramble has 48 engineers across six teams, twelve of them senior. Transfers between teams are self-selected. Over eighteen months, seven of the twelve seniors have moved onto one team, Core; two teams, Growth and Billing, now have no senior engineer at all. Nobody decided this. Asked why they moved, the seniors say the same thing: "Core is where people review properly; on Growth I was the only one who cared about review, and I was slower for it."

Paul, the engineering director, has read the transfer log and concluded the seniors are "cliquey." His proposal for next quarter: forced reallocation, two seniors per team, effective in four weeks, with transfers frozen for a year. "Spread the talent. Break up the club."

Core's lead, Ana, says the forced move will cost her three of the seven and that they will leave the company rather than go back to being the only reviewer on a team of eight. Growth's lead, meanwhile, has had two incidents this quarter that a senior reviewer would have caught.
cases.question: Is Paul's diagnosis right? What do you do about Growth and Billing without destroying what Core has?
considerations: What does Schelling's model show about mild preferences plus interdependence, and what does it not show (ledger #17)?
Is the seniors' similarity influence or selection? What does the course assume by default?
What norm lives on Core, and what does a dense cluster do for it? What happens to a norm held by one person on a team of eight (t04)?
Which of t09's branches is the job here: holding a norm, or moving skills and information?
What is the difference between sending one senior and sending two, in threshold terms?
cases.model_answer:
Decision: reject the two-per-team reallocation; send seniors into Growth and Billing in pairs for a fixed term as visible demonstrators, and keep Core above the size that holds its review norm. Draw the situation first: each senior has a mild preference for peers who review at their level; with interdependence (you are slower if you are the only one who cares), mild preferences produce extreme sorting. Schelling's model shows exactly that, and that homogeneity is weak evidence of intolerance (ledger #17) [E for the model; H that it explains this case].

t09's rule has two branches and this case sits on both. IF the job is to hold a costly norm THEN keep the unit small, dense and bounded, which Core is [E for the mechanism]. IF the job is to move a rare skill THEN build bridges, and for a resisting cluster seed inside it with more than one adopter, because a lone reviewer on a team of eight is the lone cooperator in a stag hunt, worse off for having tried (t04) [E for the model; H here]. Paul's two-per-team gives every team the Growth outcome and dissolves Core's pocket: the file's named mistake of reorganizing for cross-pollination while a young norm sits in a few dense pockets. So: two seniors move together to Growth for two quarters and two to Billing, cohorts not tokens (`05`) [H]; Core keeps three [H]; the demonstrators' reviews are visible, so the norm spreads because it visibly pays (`07`, ledger #36) [H]; their delivery targets drop for the term (`02`) [E in the tournament; V that skill spread is worth two quarters of throughput, Paul's freeze the dissent].

To Paul: the sorting is the structure's doing and will reproduce itself after any freeze; assign explicit ownership of team composition to your office, because sorting externalities have no natural owner (`05`) [V]. Balancing measure: measure the 2pq ratio for senior-junior review ties across teams; fewer cross-team ties than chance is the homophily being bridged (`10`) [E, theorem].

Switch signal: toward closure if the seeded pairs' norm fails because nobody around them adopts it, or they ask to return early; toward bridges if Core's incidents rise because rare knowledge sat with someone who left. Register entry [H]: "Growth's review-catchable incidents fall during the two quarters with a senior pair; at least two Growth engineers review at the demonstrated standard by term's end."
cases.novice_error: Break up the club, because seven seniors on one team looks like a fairness problem and a spread looks like an obvious fix. It scatters the one place the review norm is dense and recreates the lone-reviewer situation on six teams instead of two. The mirror is to protect Core until Growth and Billing are permanently junior teams with no one to catch the incidents.

cases.title: The bounty split that costs contributors every quarter
cases.scenario:
The Kestrel foundation pays a quarterly bounty pool of $20,000 to contributors of its open-source runtime. Three maintainers split it at their discretion among about 40 contributors, and post the amounts. Every quarter the forum thread on the split runs to over a hundred replies, and three to five contributors leave, usually the ones who received less than they expected. Last quarter one contributor who had merged the largest feature received the same as one who fixed typos, because the maintainers "wanted to encourage newcomers."

Kemal, the treasurer, has a fix for the next split in five weeks: "People are just greedy. Equal shares for everyone who merged anything; nobody can argue with equal." Hana, a maintainer, wants the opposite: shares proportional to lines of code merged, computed by a script, "so it's objective." A third maintainer points out that nobody has ever asked the contributors what they think a fair split is, and that the foundation's own contributors include people from several countries with different norms about pay and credit.
cases.question: What rule governs the next split, and how do you find out what "fair" means to these forty people?
considerations: What do people punish in the ultimatum game: unequal outcomes or unfair intentions? What does that say about last quarter's "encourage newcomers" split?
What do the ledger's numbers say about the fairness baseline: is there a universal 50-50, or does the content vary?
What is t05's rule for choosing a fairness baseline, and which four questions elicit it?
What does Hana's script do to unmeasured contribution (t12)? What does Kemal's equal split assume about the norm?
What does "seed early rounds deliberately" mean for the first split under a new rule?
cases.model_answer:
Decision: elicit the group's fairness norm before the next split, then publish a procedurally impartial rule built from what it says, with the first split under it chosen deliberately. Draw the game first: a repeated allocation in which recipients retaliate by exit, and people punish intended unfairness far more than unlucky outcomes (`06`, Blount 1995) [E in the lab]. Last quarter's split was read as an intention (a large feature paid the same as typo fixes), so the exits were retaliation, not greed.

t05's rule: IF you are choosing a fairness baseline THEN elicit it from the group; never a lab or 50-50 default (ledger #25). The content of fairness is local: mean ultimatum offers ran from about 26% to about 58% across fifteen small-scale societies (Henrich et al. 2001, verified), while student offers average about 40%, mode 40-50% [E]. So this month, Bicchieri's four questions anonymously: what split rule would you use; what do most contributors here consider fair; what do most think the maintainers should do; what happens when a split is seen as unfair [E for the method, design-sensitive]. Then a rule that makes the allocation procedurally impartial, removing the intention signal: a published rubric (merged changes weighted by an impact score set at merge time, before anyone knows the pool) and a lottery for ties (`06`) [E for the mechanism; H for this rubric]. Seed the first round deliberately, since first splits set the fairness attractor (`08`) [H, shown in simulation].

To Kemal: equal shares import one norm without asking. To Hana: lines of code is a partial metric that displaces review, triage and documentation and is gamed within a quarter (t12, `04`) [E as theory]. A small, stated newcomer share is legitimate if it is a visible rule rather than a surprise [V, that process fairness is a good in itself, Kemal dissenting]. Balancing measure: the norm is conditional until it survives a collapse of expectations (ledger #10), so treat the elicited baseline as the group's current norm, not its character.

Switch signal: toward norms if complaints track what contributors believe others received rather than what they value, and exits fall once the rule is public and unchanged; toward preferences if the same people complain under every rule and framing. Register entry [H]: "under a published rubric, exits after a split fall to at most one per quarter for three quarters."
cases.novice_error: Pick a rule that sounds unarguable, equal or by lines of code, because the pain is the argument and any objective rule seems to end it. Both impose a fairness content nobody elicited, and the script one pays for exactly the contribution that is easiest to fake. The mirror is to keep discretion and simply explain the reasoning better, which leaves the intention signal in every split.

cases.title: Sixteen sign-offs and one late reviewer
cases.scenario:
A monthly release of Orrery's platform requires sign-off from sixteen component owners. The release goes out when the last signature lands. Six months ago the median time from release-candidate to full sign-off was one day; it is now four, and the last two releases slipped a week. Yara, the release manager, has asked around: owners say, in nearly the same words, "There's no point rushing; someone is always late, and if I sign early and then a bug turns up I've wasted the review." Each owner's review takes about three hours if done carefully.

Yara's proposal to the VP, due Friday: a team bonus paid when a release ships on time, and a "release hero" award. The VP's instinct is a hard deadline with escalation to managers for late signatures. One component owner, Femi, suggests quietly that the problem is the sixteen, not the people: when the process had six signatories two years ago, nobody was ever more than a day late.
cases.question: What do you change about the sign-off process before the next release, and is Femi right?
considerations: What game is a release that ships when the slowest of sixteen signs? What does the lab say such groups converge to, and at what size?
What is the cost of signing early, and how does it compare with the reward for a fast release? Which does the bonus touch?
What are the two structural fixes t04 names for a large weak-link group?
What could a visible sign-off board do, and what does a leader naming the target do?
What does escalation to managers do to the shadow of the future between owners?
cases.model_answer:
Decision: Femi is right; change the aggregation rule so the release no longer waits for the slowest of sixteen, and cap the group whose minimum matters at a handful. Draw the game first: sixteen players each choosing how fast to review, and the release's timing is the minimum of their choices. That is a weak-link game with an unambiguous lab record: groups of 14-16 fell to the lowest effort within about ten rounds while fixed pairs reached the top (Van Huyck, Battalio and Beil 1990; group-size result verified, round counts background) [E]. The owners have said the mechanism aloud: signing early is wasted if someone else is late, so waiting is risk-dominant.

t04's first branch applies: IF matching is near-random, the group is large, people best-respond to what they last saw and there is no channel for commitment THEN plan for risk dominance: cap the group whose minimum matters at a handful, or change the aggregation rule from minimum to median or average. Nest the sixteen: four area leads sign the release; the other twelve sign to their lead asynchronously during the candidate week, so the release-critical minimum is over four (`06`, cap the group; `09`, nesting) [E for the group-size effect; H for this structure]. For low-risk components, silence by the deadline is consent, so a late owner delays only their own component [E for the lever in the model; V that shipping without the slowest signature is acceptable, the VP dissenting]. Then the cheap levers: re-review scoped to the diff since signing, so an early signature is never wasted [H]; Yara names the target, "two days" (`06`) [E in the lab].

To Yara: the bonus sweetens the joint payoff, the weakest lever, and pays for a measurable outcome while displacing careful review (t12, `04`) [E as theory]. To the VP: escalation makes late signatures a manager's problem and removes owners' repeated dealings with each other; it is enforcement for a trust problem. Balancing measure: the four leads are now a weak-link group of four; keep them stable and give them the board.

Switch signal: if median sign-off keeps rising toward the minimum with four leads, more components move to consent; if it falls and holds, ask whether any early signature was re-done, the lone-cooperator cost measured directly. Register entry [H]: "median candidate-to-ship under two days for three consecutive releases with four release-critical signatures."
cases.novice_error: Pay a bonus and name a hero, because the release is late and money is the obvious accelerator. The bonus touches the payoff nobody was short of (joint success) and ignores the one that decides the game (the cost of signing early), and the award turns sixteen colleagues into competitors. The mirror is the VP's deadline, which punishes the slowest signer and removes the peer accountability that could have held the group.

cases.title: The quarterly rotation to spread the culture
cases.scenario:
At Marrow, one team of six, Atlas, runs blameless incident reviews: a write-up within 24 hours of every incident, no names, a public list of fixes, read by the whole team. The other five teams, 34 engineers, do not; their incidents are discussed in private and rarely written up. Atlas's practice is eight months old and its lead, Ben, says it took five months before the team stopped flinching at writing down their own mistakes.

Mei, the COO, has seen the difference in Atlas's incident recurrence and wants the culture everywhere. Her proposal, starting next quarter: rotate 25% of every team, chosen at random, to another team every quarter, for a year. "Mix the people and the culture spreads." Ben's objection is that Atlas would lose two of six each quarter and the practice would dilute before it spread. A second team lead adds that the last person who tried to introduce write-ups on his team stopped after two months because "writing down your incident when nobody else does just makes you look bad."
cases.question: Do you support the rotation? If not, how do you get blameless reviews into the other five teams over the year?
considerations: What is the Atlas team, structurally, for an eight-month-old costly norm? What does random rotation do to the basin it sits in (t04)?
Is a blameless write-up a simple or a complex contagion? How many adopting neighbours does the lone adopter on another team have?
What does the file say about the speed of contagion under local imitation versus random mixing, and under which learning rule?
Which of t09's branches applies, and what is the difference between seeding a cohort and rotating individuals?
What has to be visible for success-biased copying to work?
cases.model_answer:
Decision: no random rotation; seed the practice into one team at a time with a pair from Atlas, keep Atlas above four, and make the practice's payoff visible so it spreads by success, not headcount. Draw the game first: writing up your own incident is costly and pays only when others do it too; the second lead's story is the lone cooperator in a stag hunt. Atlas is a dense cluster in which every member has five adopting neighbours; a cluster with density above 1 − q protects a norm inside and blocks one from outside (`10`, ledger #3) [E, theorem]. Random rotation of 25% a quarter is the t04 mistake verbatim: assuming a small group has secured the good outcome for good, then rotating people randomly across teams, which hands the basin back to risk dominance.

t09's first branch: IF the job is to hold a costly norm and spread it neighbour by neighbour THEN keep units small, dense and bounded, and when spreading to a resisting cluster build wide bridges or seed inside it. A blameless write-up is a complex contagion needing several adopting neighbours; one rotated engineer on a team of seven has zero (ledger #34) [E for the direction]. So: two Atlas engineers move together into one target team for two quarters, run its incident reviews jointly, and return; Atlas stays at four (`07`) [H]. Check the learning rule: local structure spreads cooperation only under success-copying (ledger #3, #36), so publish Atlas's recurrence numbers and follow the target team's first write-up with a visible fix within the week (`02`) [E for the mechanism; H for the effect size].

To Mei: mixing people spreads information, not a habit that punishes the first adopter. To Ben: four is the floor, and two people gone for two quarters is the price of spreading it at all [V, that spreading the practice is worth Atlas's throughput, Ben dissenting]. Balancing measure: rotate a demonstrator in from the converted team afterwards so Atlas does not become a silo [H].

Switch signal: toward closure if the seeded pair's write-ups stop because nobody around them follows; toward bridges if Atlas's practice stalls in isolation or another team invents a worse version. Register entry [H]: "the first seeded team produces write-ups within 24 hours for at least three of four incidents in its second quarter; recurrence falls."
cases.novice_error: Rotate people, because culture "lives in people" and a quarter of every team moving looks like decisive spreading. It dissolves the only cluster where the norm is dense and drops single adopters into teams where writing up your incident makes you look bad. The mirror is Ben's, unmodified: keep Atlas intact and wait for the others to notice, which they will not, because a costly norm does not jump on its own.

cases.title: A pledge round before the allocation
cases.scenario:
Eleven research groups share a quarterly allocation of GPU hours on a consortium cluster. Each group submits a request; the facilitator, Rosa, scales all requests down to fit. Every group knows that a group which overstates its need gets more after scaling, and last quarter total requests were about three times the cluster's capacity. Two groups then left a large share of their allocation unused.

Rosa's plan for the next allocation meeting in three weeks: open with a round in which each group's lead says aloud what they will request and commits, in front of the other ten, to requesting only what they will use. "Once people say it to each other's faces, they keep to it." Diego, who leads the group that underused most last quarter, is blunt: "Pledges are cheap talk. Everyone will nod and then pad their number. What we need is an audit and penalties." A third lead thinks both are overkill and the scaling formula just needs tweaking.
cases.question: Do you keep Rosa's pledge round? What has to sit beside it for it to survive past one quarter?
considerations: Does a group gain by padding when the other ten are honest? What game is that, and what does the diagnostic in t07 say to do about talk?
What did the lab find about relevant discussion before a dilemma, and what does the ledger say happens after it where defection pays?
In Bicchieri's account, what does a face-to-face pledge round create inside each lead, and why does that matter for a prisoner's dilemma?
What counts as fast detection here, and what is the cheapest graduated sanction the data already supports?
What does Diego's audit-and-penalty plan risk if it arrives without the talk?
cases.model_answer:
Decision: keep the pledge round, and pair it with by-product monitoring and an automatic graduated sanction, because the game is a prisoner's dilemma and talk alone will decay. Draw the game with t07's diagnostic: does a group gain by overstating when the other ten request honestly? Yes, it takes a larger share after scaling. So this is a prisoner's dilemma, and the second branch applies: IF a member does gain THEN still hold relevant talk before the mixed-motive decision and extract explicit promises, but pair it with what stops decay: repetition with fast detection, graduated sanctions, or a payoff change [E for the diagnostic].

Rosa is right about the first quarter: relevant face-to-face discussion is the strongest single lever on dilemma cooperation in the lab, roughly doubling it in an eight-person dilemma (Dawes, McTavish and Shaklee 1977, background; Sally 1995 and Balliet 2010 behind it) [E in the lab], because a public promise creates empirical and normative expectations that turn the dilemma toward coordination for human subjects (`08`) [E for the lab effect; H for persistence here]. Diego is right about the third quarter: where defection dominates, cheap talk decays without sanctions or repetition (ledger #12) [E]. So beside the round: Rosa publishes each group's requested hours against hours used, monitoring as a by-product of use, not an audit (`09`) [E for the principle in bounded commons; H for transfer]; unused allocation reduces next quarter's request ceiling by the unused amount, by formula, so nobody has to be the punisher (`09`) [E]; a cheap dispute channel for cancelled projects [E for dispute forums].

To Diego: penalties without the talk land on groups merely uncertain how much to ask, lowering expectations and manufacturing the padding they fear. Balancing measure: the sanction is a ceiling, not a fine, and the round repeats every quarter, because repetition keeps the promise alive [V, that assurance should lead and enforcement follow, Diego dissenting].

Switch signal: measure requests-to-capacity at the meeting and two quarters on. If the ratio falls and drifts back up with pledge-keepers ending up with less than padders, decay is the dilemma's signature and the ceiling tightens; if padding comes in waves after a group is seen to underuse, it is doubt, and the fix is more visible usage data. Register entry [H]: "total requests below 1.5 times capacity within two quarters of pledge round plus published usage; unused share below 10%."
cases.novice_error: Choose between Rosa and Diego, because the meeting frames it as talk versus teeth. Talk alone is a first-quarter fix for a game where padding pays; penalties alone signal distrust to groups that would have kept a promise. The mirror is the third lead's: adjust the formula and treat padding as an arithmetic problem, leaving the dilemma untouched.

cases.title: Weekend messages nobody likes
cases.scenario:
Lantern is a 90-person remote company. Weekend Slack messages are routine: an anonymous survey run by the people team found that 78% of respondents dislike sending them and 85% believe most colleagues expect a reply within a few hours. Tomas, the CEO, sends several every weekend, usually prefixed "no rush." Two managers have told their teams privately to ignore weekend messages, and both teams still reply.

The people team has drafted a "right to disconnect" policy for the handbook, to be announced at the next all-hands in two weeks. Sofia, a team lead, says the policy is beside the point: "This is a values problem. Run a workshop on boundaries and let people commit to them." A third view, from an engineer: "Nobody wants this, everybody does it, and it will stop the day Tomas stops." The people team's own count shows weekend traffic is highest in the two teams whose managers told them to ignore it, because their managers keep replying to Tomas.
cases.question: What do you do at the all-hands, and what happens to the policy and the workshop?
considerations: Classify the norm with Bicchieri's taxonomy: what sustains weekend replying, empirical expectations, normative expectations or both? What does the survey show about the normative ones?
What is the gap between private attitudes and perceived norms called, and what collapses it?
Is this a moral norm that a values workshop could address, or a social norm? What does t05 say to assume until proven otherwise?
Who is the credible source in this reference network, and what is Tomas's "no rush" doing in Henrich's terms?
What convention (a self-enforcing default) could replace the norm?
cases.model_answer:
Decision: make the attitude gap common knowledge at the all-hands through the one credible source, Tomas, backed by a visible change in his own behaviour and a scheduled-send default; shelve the workshop and shrink the policy to a one-line convention. Draw the situation with Bicchieri's taxonomy (ledger #11): weekend replying is a social norm held up by empirical expectations (everyone sees the messages) and by normative expectations the survey shows are false: 85% believe others expect a reply, 78% dislike sending. That is pluralistic ignorance (`08`, `03`) [E for the phenomenon].

t05's rule: IF you are diagnosing a norm THEN assume it is conditional until it survives a collapse of expectations, and never run values workshops for a norm not first diagnosed as moral rather than social (ledger #10). This norm is social: nobody holds weekend replying as a value; they hold a belief about others. So Sofia's workshop is aimed at the wrong bin, and the policy is a memo (t01). Tomas publishes the two survey numbers and says he was wrong, the gap made common knowledge by a credible source [E for the diagnosis; H for the intervention].
