Then a costly display: he stops sending weekend messages and says so, because "no rush" from the CEO is a credibility-enhancing display pointing the wrong way; the message beats the prefix (`01`) [E for the mechanism]. Then a convention needing no heroism: scheduled-send as the default outside working hours, so the cue that fires the script disappears (`08`) [H, the cue-to-norm mapping must be tested locally].

To Sofia: a workshop produces commitments about a norm people already privately reject; what they lack is a belief about the other 89. That the company owes people their weekends is a value [V, Sofia dissenting only on the means]. Balancing measure, from t10: publish the attitude ("most of us would rather not"), pair it with approval, and never publish "most of us send weekend messages" [E for the pairing rule].

Switch signal: toward norms, confirmed, if weekend traffic tracks what people believe others do and falls within weeks; toward preferences if it persists in a team whose members can state the numbers and whose lead sends nothing, and the lever moves to hours. Register entry [H]: "weekend messages fall by more than half within six weeks of the announcement and Tomas's stop; the four-question survey shows perceived expectation aligned with private attitude."
cases.novice_error: Announce the policy and run the workshop, because a handbook clause and a values session are what companies do about culture. Both leave the belief about the other 89 exactly where it was, and the CEO's weekend messages will refute the clause by Saturday. The mirror is to publish the raw behaviour count as a wake-up call, which tells everyone the norm is universal.

cases.title: CI quotas with automatic lockout
cases.scenario:
Fourteen teams share one continuous-integration cluster at Tessellate. Two teams, Search and Mobile, have started running very large test matrices on every commit; median queue time for everyone else has gone from four minutes to forty. Ingrid, who leads the platform team that owns the cluster, has written the fix: a per-team quota of compute minutes per day, with automatic lockout for the rest of the day when a team exceeds it. It ships in two weeks. There has been no consultation; "we own the cluster, and consultation is how nothing ships."

Three team leads have objected in a thread. One says the quota will lock out a team mid-incident. Another says teams will simply stand up their own runners and stop using the shared cluster at all. Search's lead says he had no idea his matrix was the cause, because nobody can see per-team usage. Ingrid's manager wants the queue fixed before the quarterly review in six weeks.
cases.question: Does the quota ship as designed? What do you change about who writes the rule and what the cluster shows?
considerations: What kind of resource is a CI cluster (subtractable, costly to exclude from)? Does a team gain by running a big matrix when others restrain themselves?
Can the fourteen teams currently observe each other's use? Which of Ostrom's channels does the course say to fix first?
What does t06 predict for a rule designed by the platform team and enforced automatically, and what is the exit option?
What is a graduated ladder for a compute overrun, and what is a nuclear first strike?
What role does the platform team keep under Ostrom's principle 7?
cases.model_answer:
Decision: the platform team designs the structure and ships the visibility this week; the fourteen leads write the operational quota rule within three weeks; automatic lockout becomes a graduated ladder. Draw the game first: a CI cluster is a common-pool resource, subtractable and costly to exclude from, and a team gains by running a large matrix while others restrain, so at the margin this is a real prisoner's dilemma, (ledger #13) [E]. Search's lead did not know he was the cause because nobody can see per-team usage: the observation channel is broken, and Ostrom's file says fix that before treating anything as free-riding [E].

t06's rule: IF the group is large or the problem is an externality members cannot see THEN design the structure (boundaries, by-product monitoring, a graduated ladder, a cheap dispute forum), but hand operational rules to members within weeks. Ingrid's lockout skips to external authorship, whose prediction is compliance only while enforced (Cardenas, background) plus exit, teams stand up their own runners [E for the crowding-out pattern; H here]. In order: this week, a per-team usage dashboard on the cluster's front page, monitoring as a by-product of use (`09`) [E for the principle in bounded cases; H for transfer, scope flagged]. Then the ladder: warning at 80% of share, deprioritized queue above 100%, throttling only for repeated overruns, never a same-day lockout, the nuclear first strike that hits a team mid-incident [E for graduated sanctions in durable cases]. Then authorship: the leads set shares against capacity, with the platform team as backstop and data source; its ownership is what makes the leads' rule legitimate (principle 7) [E for the principle; V that the pen belongs to those bound by the rule, Ingrid dissenting].

To Ingrid: consultation on a voluntary practice is how nothing ships; consultation on the rule that fixes a dilemma is welcomed by people who would not have complied voluntarily (`05`) [H]. Balancing measure: the leads have three weeks; if they cannot agree, the platform team's draft ladder applies as the default.

Switch signal: toward design if the fourteen cannot agree by the date; toward self-governance if teams comply only under throttling or appeal every sanction upward. Register entry [H]: "median queue time under ten minutes within six weeks, with the quota rule authored by the leads and no team leaving the shared cluster."
cases.novice_error: Ship the lockout, because the platform team owns the cluster, the fix is technically simple, and the review is in six weeks. It fixes the queue for as long as the lockout is enforced and pushes the biggest users off the cluster entirely. The mirror is to hand the whole thing to a fourteen-lead working group with no structure, no data and no default, and watch the queue stay at forty minutes while they meet.

cases.title: Staff-only moderation and the appeals queue
cases.scenario:
Quill is a question-and-answer platform with about 60,000 registered users and four staff moderators who handle every report, from duplicate questions to harassment. Bans are issued by whichever staff member picks up the report; the community has documented cases where near-identical behaviour got a warning from one moderator and a permanent ban from another. Appeals have tripled in a year, the moderation backlog is eleven days, and a group of 40 long-standing users has petitioned for elected community moderators.

Leo, Head of Trust and Safety, has to present a plan to the board in six weeks. His position: "We cannot hand enforcement to users. It's a legal exposure, and volunteers will play favourites." His plan is two more staff moderators and a longer written policy. The petitioners' lead, Marguerite, says the community already runs an unofficial flagging network in a chat group that catches most spam before staff do, and that staff bans are the only thing on the platform nobody understands.
cases.question: What do you propose to the board, and what do the four staff moderators do afterward?
considerations: Which enforcement decisions on Quill are operational (duplicates, tagging, spam) and which carry the legal exposure Leo names? Must they have the same author?
What does Ostrom's principle 7 say about the surrounding authority's role, and what does nesting look like on a platform?
Why are inconsistent sanctions worse than lenient ones (`06`, intention versus outcome)?
What does the unofficial flagging network tell you about where by-product monitoring already exists?
What does the ledger say about the transfer of Ostrom's principles to digital commons?
cases.model_answer:
Decision: propose a nested moderation system to the board: community moderators author and apply the operational tier, staff keep the flagrant and legal tier as recognised backstop, and both work from a published ladder and log. Draw the situation first: a platform of 60,000 is not one group, and four staff cannot observe it; the community's unofficial flagging network is where by-product monitoring already exists (`09`) [E for the principle; H for transfer to a digital commons, flagged per ledger #29]. The inconsistency is the acute damage: people punish intended unfairness far more than unlucky outcomes (`06`) [E in the lab], which is why appeals have tripled.

t06's rule: IF the group already communicates, observes itself and can change its rules THEN fix those channels first, then let members craft operational rules against the eight principles, with external authority as recognition, backstop and data; IF an external authority insists on writing the rules THEN expect compliance only while enforced. Leo's plan is the platform default, a rulebook written centrally and treated as someone else's law [E for the pattern; H here]. Tier by exposure. Tier one, operational: elected community moderators, a published graduated ladder (note, short restriction, longer restriction), a public sanctions log [E for graduated sanctions, supported in the 91-study review (Cox et al. 2010, verified); H for a platform]. Tier two, flagrant and legal: staff only, fast track, same log. Appeals go first to a peer panel of three community moderators [E for dispute forums]. Principle 7 is the board's job: an explicit statement that the community may govern tier one, so its sanctions cannot be appealed over its head [E for the principle; V that polycentric arrangements beat one decision centre, Leo dissenting].

To Leo: tiering answers the legal point; the ladder and log answer favouritism, since a published first step is harder to bend than a discretionary ban. Balancing measure: the community tier needs a written boundary (who may vote, serve, for how long) naming whom it excludes and why [V], and a dated first revision.

Switch signal: toward design if elected moderators cannot agree a ladder within a quarter; toward more self-governance if tier-one sanctions are still appealed upward or staff keep overriding the panel. Register entry [H]: "appeals per hundred sanctions halve and backlog falls under three days within two quarters, with no rise in tier-two incidents."
cases.novice_error: Hire two more staff and lengthen the policy, because moderation is a liability and the board wants control. Six staff cannot observe 60,000 users any better than four, and the longer policy makes inconsistency more visible, not rarer. The mirror is to hand everything, harassment included, to elected volunteers with no recognition from the platform, so the first serious case is appealed to a legal team that never agreed to the arrangement.

cases.title: The documentation norm that never crossed the liaison
cases.scenario:
Two departments at Halyard share a data warehouse. Data Engineering, 30 people, adopted a norm a year ago: every dataset has a named owner and a README, and a pull request that adds a dataset without them is not merged. Adoption inside Data is complete. Product Analytics, 45 people, creates about half of the new datasets and has adopted none of it: zero owners, zero READMEs, after twelve months in which Omar, the one analyst who sits with Data Engineering, has presented the norm at three Product all-hands and posted the template four times.

Elif, Head of Data, wants the CTO to mandate the norm company-wide with a merge check. Omar says he is tired of being "the docs guy" and that his colleagues agree with him in the meeting and do nothing after. Product Analytics' lead, Chen, points out that his analysts review each other's work, almost never Data's, and that an analyst who writes a README is the only one on her squad who does, "and it's not obvious what she gets for it."
cases.question: Why has a norm that is universal on one side of Omar not crossed to the other, and what do you do instead of the mandate?
considerations: What is Omar, in network terms? What crosses a single bridge and what does not (ledger #34)?
What does the analyst who writes a README get, and how many of her review neighbours also do? What is q for her?
Which of `10`'s levers lower q, seed inside a cluster and widen a bridge, and what does each look like here?
What does the ledger say about clusters blocking a norm from outside while protecting one inside?
What does t13 say about running an expectations campaign across clusters that cannot see each other?
cases.model_answer:
Decision: stop evangelising through Omar, build three parallel ties between the departments, seed inside the most cohesive analytics squad, and lower the cost of the norm; hold the mandate in reserve. Draw the situation first: two dense clusters, one bridge. Owners and READMEs are a costly behaviour whose value depends on neighbours doing it too, so it is a complex contagion: information crosses one weak tie, costly behaviour needs several adopting neighbours and wide bridges (ledger #34) [E for the direction]. The analyst who writes a README has zero adopting neighbours among those who review her, so she sits below q = b/(a+b) and is the lone cooperator (`10`, theorem; t04) [E for the theorem; H for the value of q].

t09's first branch applies: IF the job is to hold a costly norm and spread it to a resisting cluster THEN build wide bridges or seed inside it. Lower q: a README template the tooling generates from the schema and an owner field filled by default, so one adopting neighbour tips a node (`10`) [E for the lever in the model; H for its size]. Seed inside: the analytics squad with the most joins to Data's tables co-owns three shared datasets with two Data engineers, who become its review neighbours [E for the mechanism; H for the choice of squad]. Widen the bridge: joint review of cross-department datasets, three parallel ties where there was one [E for bridges being weak and decaying unattended].

To Elif: a merge check written by Data and applied to Product produces the thinnest README that passes, complied with while checked (t06) [E for the pattern]; keep it as the dated fallback. To Omar: three all-hands were an expectations campaign across clusters that cannot see each other, which t13 says never to run [E]. Balancing measure: cap seeding at one squad per quarter so Data's own cluster keeps its density [V, that cross-department flow is worth some of Data's review budget, Elif dissenting].

Switch signal: toward structure, confirmed, if adoption in the seeded squad rises once two neighbours adopt; toward expectations if, with tooling and neighbours in place, analysts can state the norm and still believe nobody in Product expects it. Register entry [H]: "the seeded squad reaches owner-and-README on at least three of four new datasets within one quarter; a second squad follows within two, without a merge check."
cases.novice_error: Escalate to a mandate, because a year of evangelism has failed and a merge check reaches all 45 analysts on Monday. It reaches them as a rule from another department and gets the minimum document that passes. The mirror is to send Omar to a fourth all-hands with a better slide, which is the same single tie carrying the same information to a cluster that has heard it.

cases.title: Show of hands after the two most senior said yes
cases.scenario:
The architecture guild at Sorrel, twenty engineers, decides on cross-cutting technical changes. Last month it voted on migrating the message queue to a new system. The two most senior members spoke first, both in favour, at some length. The chair then called a show of hands: 18 in favour, 2 against. Three weeks later, a junior member tells Priyanka, the guild chair, that "at least half the room had doubts" and that the two who voted against have been treated coolly since. Two teams have quietly deferred their part of the migration.

Priyanka's plan for the next guild meeting in two weeks: re-run the vote after a reminder about the guild's value of candour, and ask the two seniors to say explicitly that dissent is welcome. "If people know it's safe to disagree, they will." A senior member thinks the vote should stand: "18-2 is a mandate; doubts after the fact are just cold feet." The migration's first milestone is due in six weeks.
cases.question: Do you re-run the vote, and how? Is the problem what people expected of each other, or the way the decision was structured?
considerations: What is a decision in which people signal publicly in sequence after two confident signals? Which kind of copying is this (ledger #19), and what is its fix?
In the urn model, how often does a cascade go wrong with fairly accurate signals, and what does that say about 18-2?
Which of t13's branches applies: is this one reference network with an attitude-expectation gap, or a structural problem in who sees what signal first?
What do `03` and `10` prescribe for sequential public decisions, and what does a "candour" reminder change about the sequence?
How would you find out whether the 18 believed the migration was right or believed the seniors did?
cases.model_answer:
Decision: re-run the decision, not the vote: collect private written positions before any discussion, reveal them together, have the seniors speak last, and drop the candour reminder. Draw the situation first: twenty people signalling in public, in sequence, after two long confident signals from the most senior. That is an informational cascade (ledger #19, the copying kind whose fix is to collect private signals first): once two people you respect have said yes, following is individually reasonable whatever your own signal, and the show of hands records the cascade, not the room. The urn model puts the chance of a wrong cascade at about 1/5 with signals 2/3 accurate (`10` ch 16, a computation, illustrative) [E for the mechanism; the figure is a model].

t13's rule sorts the fix. The failure is not an attitude-expectation gap a credible publication would close; it is the order in which private signals became public. So the structure branch applies: IF the outcome is decided by who sees the signal first THEN change the structure and let expectations follow; for any sequential public decision, collect private judgments first, reveal them simultaneously, reverse speaking order (`10`, `03`) [E]. Priyanka's candour reminder is an expectations intervention aimed at a structural cause: it invites dissent and then runs the same sequence, seniors first. Concretely: written positions and main risk submitted beforehand; the distribution published before anyone speaks; discussion opens with the risks; an assigned credible dissenter; seniors last; the decision re-taken on the same basis (`03`) [E for each mechanism; H for the package].

To the senior member: if the private-first count comes back 18-2, the room did agree and the migration proceeds with the deferring teams told the count [V, that a decision reached by independent signals is worth two weeks against a milestone, which he disputes]. Balancing measure: `11` adds that persistent disagreement between the deferring teams and the guild on the same data indicates different priors, aligned by shared definitions, not re-voting [H].

Switch signal: toward structure, confirmed, if the private-first count differs materially from 18-2; toward expectations if it matches and the deferring teams still doubt the room, and the lever becomes publishing it credibly. Register entry [H]: "private-first positions are collected before every guild decision; on this migration, the private count is published and at least one deferring team recommits or the decision is revised."
cases.novice_error: Re-run the show of hands after a speech about candour, because the problem looks like courage and a leader can ask for courage. The sequence that produced the cascade is untouched, and the two seniors still speak first. The mirror is to let 18-2 stand as a mandate and push the milestone, then discover at week six that half the room built the migration they did not believe in.

cases.title: Two squads, same dashboard, opposite conclusions
cases.scenario:
At Cinder, the Growth squad and the Retention squad read the same weekly product dashboard every Monday and, for three months, have reached opposite conclusions. Growth: activation is fine, push acquisition. Retention: activation is broken, pause acquisition. Both cite the same activation chart. Each squad has its own definition of "activated" in its own notebooks, and each believes the other's is wrong. The argument has consumed part of every planning meeting, and the quarterly plan is due in four weeks.

Chen, VP of Data, proposes two more dashboards and a "source of truth" document listing every metric. "More data will settle it." Growth's lead says the squads should just each pursue their own conclusion. Retention's lead wants an executive to rule. A data scientist points out that the two squads have never sat in the same room to agree what "activated" means, and that each squad's definition makes its own conclusion follow.
cases.question: Is this a disagreement more data can settle? What do you put in place before the quarterly plan?
considerations: Two groups reading the same data and reaching opposite conclusions every week: in Gintis's terms, what differs between them? What does he say fixes it?
Is the current Monday argument a stable pattern (a stability test)? What does anyone gain by conceding?
What is the public signal that would tell both squads which equilibrium is in play, and who authors it?
What does t03 say to do when the signal exists and compliance is still low?
Which of the three proposals (more dashboards, go separate ways, executive ruling) is a choreographer, and which is a poster?
cases.model_answer:
Decision: name the signal, not the data: one definition of "activated," one owner, and a written decision rule that both squads accept before the plan, authored jointly in a room. Draw the situation first and check stability: the Monday argument is stable because nobody gains by conceding; each squad's definition makes its conclusion follow, so this is two equilibria with no shared cue. Gintis's diagnosis (`11`) fits: persistent disagreement across sub-teams on the same data indicates different priors, fixed by cultural alignment (shared definitions, training, narrative), not more data [H, from the common-priors model].

t03's rule: IF the pattern passes the stability test but the group is not there THEN stop reasoning people toward it and name the signal: a public cue that tells each person which equilibrium is in play; ambiguity, not incentives, is the usual failure. This is the choreographer idea: a public signal aligns conjectures where rationality alone cannot (ledger #31, framework, never "the unification") [E for the formal relation; H that this layer is what bites here]. Concretely: the two leads and the data scientist define "activated" once, give it one owner, and pair it with a decision rule ("if seven-day activation is below X, acquisition spend is capped until it recovers") that both squads sign before they know this week's number (`05`) [E for the mechanism; H for the threshold]. Then Bicchieri's layer: IF the signal exists and compliance is still low THEN measure the expectations; ask each squad what it thinks the other will do when the rule bites, because a choreographer nobody believes is a poster (`08`) [E for expectations as the mechanism].

To Retention: an executive ruling is a signal imposed from outside both reference networks, followed while watched (t06) [E for the pattern; H here]. Balancing measure: the definition is dated and revisable by the two squads together, not by Data alone [V, Chen dissenting because he holds that Data should own metrics].

Switch signal (t11): toward beliefs, confirmed, if the squads converge within weeks of the shared definition under unchanged incentives; toward preferences or constraints if they still diverge with one definition, which means the goals genuinely conflict and the fix is the budget rule, not the metric. Register entry [H]: "one activation definition, one owner and a signed decision rule before the quarterly plan; planning meetings stop re-litigating activation within two cycles."
cases.novice_error: Build more dashboards, because the argument is about a chart and charts are what the data team makes. Both squads will read the new charts through the definitions that produced the disagreement. The mirror is to ask an executive to pick a winner, which ends the meeting and leaves two definitions alive in two sets of notebooks.

cases.title: Nobody owns core-lib
cases.scenario:
`core-lib` is a shared library used by eight teams at Wren. The team that wrote it was dissolved eighteen months ago, and since then it has no owner. Pull requests to it either sit unreviewed for weeks or become fights: two teams, Payments and Catalog, each behave as if they own it, revert each other's changes, and in the last quarter three production incidents traced to conflicting changes merged the same week. Six other teams contribute occasionally and avoid the fights. There is no CODEOWNERS file, no release process, and no forum where a disputed change is decided.

Mara, the CTO, has been asked to assign an owner and has declined twice: "Ownership should emerge from whoever cares most. If I assign it, the other team stops contributing." Payments' lead wants ownership because they make the most changes. Catalog's lead says Payments would break Catalog's use cases within a month. The next incident review is in three weeks, and the platform director wants a decision before it.
cases.question: Run the full diagnostic path. What is the game, which equilibrium is missing, what structure holds it, and what accountability does it need? What do you tell Mara?
considerations: Two teams contesting a resource, each escalating: what game is that, and what is the evolutionarily stable convention for it (`11`)?
What does Ostrom's first principle say about ambiguous membership and resource boundaries, and what does the course say it is the commonest cause of?
What is the public signal here (t03), and does it matter whether the assignment is "fair" or merely salient (ledger #32)?
Who should hold the pen on core-lib's operational rules once an owner exists (t06), and at what unit size (t14)?
Why does "let it emerge" not work for a convention among eight teams (`07`)?
cases.model_answer:
Decision: assign an owner now by a public, impartial rule, and surround it with a small council, a cheap dispute forum and by-product monitoring; tell Mara emergence has had eighteen months. First, the game: Payments and Catalog are in a Hawk-Dove contest; the evolutionarily stable resolution is a bourgeois convention, "owner wins," which needs ownership to be salient, not fair (`11`, ledger #32) [E as a model; H for organizations]. Ambiguous membership violates Ostrom's first principle, the commonest structural cause of decay (`09`) [E].

Second, the signal, t03's rule: IF the pattern passes the stability test but the group is not there THEN name the signal, a public cue that tells each person which equilibrium is in play, because ambiguity, not incentives, is the failure. The signal is a CODEOWNERS file and a written rule for who decides a disputed change; assign clear owners even when the assignment is somewhat arbitrary (`11`) [E for the bourgeois-strategy results; H here]. Make the rule procedurally impartial so it reads as a rule, not an intention (`06`): the team with the most merged changes over the past year owns it, reviewed annually, Payments now [E for intention-sensitivity; V that a salient owner by rule beats a contested "fair" outcome, Mara dissenting]. Third, the structure (t06, t14): the owner holds the pen on operational rules, but a council of one representative per consuming team, eight people, meets monthly, the unit size at which repeated dealings work [E for nesting in Ostrom's cases; H for transfer to code], and a council-written compatibility rule as the cheap local dispute forum [E for the principle]. Fourth, accountability (t12): a reviewer of record on every merge and a public note plus revert as the graduated first sanction [E; H for this design].

To Mara: emergent conventions among eight teams are arbitrary and may fork (`07`), and this one forked into two [H]. Balancing measure: a dated revision of ownership in a year and a stated exit for consumers, because a boundary that gives one team the pen excludes seven [V].

Switch signal: if Payments and Catalog still revert each other with file and rule in place, the signal is not believed, so measure expectations before changing anything else. Register entry [H]: "no cross-team revert on core-lib for two quarters after CODEOWNERS plus council; contributions from the six other teams do not fall."
cases.novice_error: Wait for ownership to emerge, because assigning it looks like taking sides and Mara's reasoning sounds principled. Eighteen months of emergence produced two claimants and three incidents; the convention that ends a Hawk-Dove fight is salience, and nobody can make themselves salient without a fight. The mirror is to hand core-lib to Payments outright, with no council, no compatibility rule and no forum, and lose seven contributing teams to the exact fear Catalog named.
